title: Key Questions on Energy and AI (World Energy Outlook Special Report) - Executive summary
date_evidence: the IEA's "Key Questions on Energy and AI" report was launched on April 16, 2026
key_claim: Updated IEA projections see data centre electricity consumption roughly doubling from 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030, around 3% of global electricity demand by then; providing reliable onsite gas-fired electricity to data centres requires overbuilding generation by 30% to 70% relative to demand; the IEA recommends reforming connection queues and exploring non-firm grid connections and demand response so data centres move from grid loads to grid resources.
frame_summary: The IEA argues the AI buildout faces tightening physical bottlenecks across power and equipment, and that flexible, non-firm grid integration - not just more generation - is central to absorbing data-centre load.
notes: Tier 1 IEA analysis; used for the power-demand and grid-integration context the water signal sits beneath.

title: Data Centers Water Footprint: The Need for More Transparency (Privette, Barros & Cai)
date_evidence: Privette et al. publication titled "Data Centers Water Footprint: The Need for More Transparency" was published in AGU Advances on February 27, 2026
key_claim: Peer-reviewed analysis in AGU Advances argues the water footprint of data centres is multi-faceted, spanning direct on-site cooling and the larger indirect water embedded in electricity generation and the hardware supply chain, and that the absence of standardised, transparent reporting prevents accurate assessment of cumulative basin-level impacts.
frame_summary: The authors argue data centres' true water burden is dominated by hidden indirect use and cannot be managed without standardised public disclosure.
notes: Tier 1 peer-reviewed research; received 03/10/2025, accepted 30/01/2026, published 27/02/2026 (AGU Advances vol 7, e2025AV002140).

title: Durbin Introduces the Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act (S.4213)
key_claim: The Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act would require data centres to disclose energy and water use; the release notes the IEA estimate that a 100-megawatt data centre may consume about the same water as 2,600 households and that many proposed centres are more than ten times that size; there are roughly 4,000 active US data centres with about 3,000 more planned or under construction; many operators have purchased water and energy rights decades into the future; the bill directs reporting to EPA, DOE and USDA and allows fines for non-compliance.
frame_summary: Durbin argues that opaque data-centre water and energy use is shifting costs and risks onto communities, justifying mandatory federal-state disclosure.
notes: Tier 1 (US Senate). Source for water-rights-bought-ahead and the install-base counts; legislation itself is an early indicator.

title: Data Centers and Water Fact Sheet
date_evidence:
Data Centers and Water Fact Sheet
January 2026
key_claim: Citing Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the fact sheet states US data centres directly consumed about 66 billion litres of water in 2023 and that the 176 TWh of electricity they used the same year drove roughly 800 billion litres of water consumed indirectly through power generation - indirect use roughly an order of magnitude larger; about two-thirds of data centres built since 2022 sit in water-stressed regions; in constrained supplies, data-centre development may require long-term water supply agreements or the acquisition of water rights; closed-loop, direct-to-chip and immersion cooling are low-to-no water, and NVIDIA's Vera Rubin racks announced in January 2026 can be cooled at 45C without chillers, so newer AI-specific facilities are likely to reduce direct water use.
frame_summary: ELI argues that because most data-centre water use is indirect and set by the local generation mix, water and energy planning must be coordinated, even as next-generation cooling cuts the direct share.
notes: Tier 2 institutional. Structural anchor (Jan 2026, 3-6m band) for the indirect-dominates-direct framing; also the load-bearing source for the cooling-efficiency counter-argument.

title: From Energy Use to Air Quality, the Many Ways Data Centers Affect US Communities
key_claim: WRI reports that by 2028 AI-related US data centres could require up to 32 billion gallons of water annually, roughly enough to support 360,000 households' indoor use; two-thirds of data centres built or in development since 2022 are in water-stressed areas such as southern Arizona, the Colorado River Basin and Texas; governance responses include water-use monitoring and public disclosure, drought contingency planning, site-specific water risk assessments and reclaimed-wastewater use; and more than $64 billion of projects were delayed or cancelled between May 2024 and March 2025 amid organised local opposition.
frame_summary: WRI argues that whether the data-centre boom harms communities turns on governance choices over water, energy, siting and disclosure rather than on the buildout itself.
notes: Tier 2 institutional research; quantification anchor for forward water demand and the community-opposition figure.

title: Most new U.S. AI data centers are being built in drought zones - two-thirds of 809 planned projects set for areas with water shortages
key_claim: A new water-demand analysis finds about two-thirds of 809 planned US data-centre projects - 517 - are sited on land that has been in drought over the past year, and that direct cooling is roughly 4% of AI's overall water footprint, with power generation and chip fabrication accounting for the remainder.
frame_summary: The article argues the water debate is mis-framed around cooling when generation and fabrication dominate the footprint, and that new siting is colliding with drought geography.
notes: Tier 3 quality tech journalism; drought-siting quantification (809 planned, 517 in drought) and the cooling-is-only-4% framing.

title: Lawmakers advance bill to give state additional oversight of new data center water use
key_claim: Pennsylvania lawmakers advanced a bill requiring data-centre developers to report expected water use, its source, and the temperature of water taken in and returned, and to show no foreseeable adverse impact on water quality and quantity, with the Department of Environmental Protection empowered to reject projects judged harmful; it is one of several state-level efforts to create oversight of data-centre water use.
frame_summary: The report argues that states are moving to make water-impact disclosure a precondition of data-centre approval, with regulators empowered to refuse projects.
notes: Tier 3 public-media journalism; early-indicator anchor for water-permitting becoming a gating approval at state level.
